headline: Week in Politics: Trump's Thanksgiving messaging; Congress' pre-holiday to-do list
author: Scott Simon

paragraphs.text: Week in Politics: Trump's Thanksgiving messaging; Congress' pre-holiday to-do list We look at President Trump's messaging over Thanksgiving, as well as what Congress can get done before the holidays.
Politics
We look at President Trump's messaging over Thanksgiving, as well as what Congress can get done before the holidays.
SCOTT SIMON, HOST:

President Trump was busy over Thanksgiving. He pardoned turkeys. He spoke to U.S. troops. And in a lengthy post on Truth Social, he attacked adversaries, Somali immigrants and even jobs data that he didn't like. NPR political reporter Elena Moore joins us. Elena, thanks for being with us.
ELENA MOORE, BYLINE: Good morning, Scott. Happy to be here.

SIMON: And also to you. President Trump also posted angry messages about reporters. He shared an AI image of himself with a big red veto stamp, labeled Veto Corleone, as in vetoing a bill. How were these holiday messages received?

MOORE: Yeah. You know, this is far from the first time that we've seen Trump break with tradition on a holiday. He did this last Thanksgiving, too. He railed against immigrants and trashed Democrat leaders in a long Truth Social post. But, Scott, this Thanksgiving weekend comes at a pretty different moment for the president and his party. You know, Republicans are fresh off a bruising midterm loss where they saw Trump's 2024 coalition fracture. So the president making baseless fraud claims and fixating on partisan differences and culture-war issues isn't new, but we know what voters are really craving right now is a focus on the meat-and-potatoes issues.
SIMON: Like the economy.
MOORE: Yeah.
SIMON: And the Trump administration has proposed new tariffs on 14 U.S. trade partners, including China, the EU, India and more. What do we know about these tariffs?

MOORE: Yeah. The proposed tariff rates range depending on the country and could go as high as 40% on Chinese goods, for example. We don't know when exactly they could be implemented, and rates could change depending on negotiations between countries. Remember, though, the Supreme Court struck down Trump's earlier tariffs, and he's been trying to find ways to replace those import taxes ever since. And the White House says these tariffs are in response to unfair trading practices, but polls show politically this has been a losing issue. You know, according to midterm exit polls, 66% of Americans believe Trump's tariff policies have hurt the national economy. And we should say, you know, trying to undo some of these tariffs is going to be a focus for Democrats when they retake a majority in Congress next year.
SIMON: And let me ask you about that.

SIMON: The caucus in the House of Representatives seems to be falling behind Hakeem Jeffries to be the next House speaker. More complicated for another New York Democrat in the Senate, where there does seem to be some contention over who should be the next majority leader.

MOORE: Yeah, yeah. Hakeem Jeffries is going to be working with a historically large majority in the House next term. Over in the Senate, it's going to be a smaller margin for dissent, and the leadership election may be an early test for that. It's a race currently between Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland. Schumer has been the top Democrat in the Senate since 2017. He says he has enough votes from his colleagues to win.

Van Hollen, on the other hand, is positioning himself as more of a populist alternative, invoking similar messaging we heard on the campaign trail this cycle, you know, where we saw successful Senate candidates make no secret of their dissatisfaction with the party establishment. And, Scott, that's something Schumer is very much a part of. So that vote will be done by secret ballot, and it's set for Tuesday.
SIMON: The current Congress, the outgoing one, still has a lot to do, don't they?

MOORE: Yeah. I mean, the biggest thing is we are once again on shutdown watch. Senate Republicans are going to need to have some buy-in from Democrats if they want to pass a spending bill. But there are divides over whether that bill should include funding for the Iran war. Democrats campaigned on ending the conflict when they retake a majority. But some lawmakers think that should - you know, they should take action now. That's - you know, there's not a lot of time to reach consensus here. Government funding is set to run out on December 11.
SIMON: NPR's Elena Moore. Thanks so much for being with us today.
MOORE: Thanks, Scott.
